units.t: Hoaxes, Frauds & Mistakes. Episode two.
In this episode: Piltdown Man: the fake fossil that fooled science for 40 years, Ern Malley: the poet who never lived and Art forgery: the con artists who fooled the experts.
Part one. Piltdown Man: the fake fossil that fooled science for 40 years.
For four decades, a skull from an English gravel pit was hailed as a key link in human evolution.
It was a forgery, and the reasons experts believed it are the real lesson.
A discovery in Sussex.

In December 1912 Charles Dawson, a solicitor and keen amateur fossil collector, and Arthur Smith Woodward, a leading geologist at the British Museum, Natural History, presented a sensational find to the Geological Society of London.
From a gravel pit near Piltdown in Sussex came fragments of a skull and part of a jawbone with two worn teeth, along with animal fossils and crude stone tools.
Woodward's reconstruction showed a creature with a large, humanlike braincase and an apelike jaw.
It was named Eoanthropus dawsoni, ‘Dawson's dawn man’.
Newspapers celebrated the earliest Englishman, and many experts accepted Piltdown as a vital link between apes and humans.
Expectation and missing evidence.
Piltdown confirmed what many scientists already thought: that a large brain evolved before other human features.
National pride played a part too.
Germany had the Neanderthal remains and the Heidelberg jaw, and France had Cro-Magnon skeletons, but Britain had little of comparable importance.
There were warning signs.
The jaw was broken exactly where it would have shown whether it belonged with the skull: the joint and the chin were missing.
Some scientists, especially in the United States and France, argued early that skull and jaw came from different creatures.
But most researchers saw only plaster casts, which could not show tool marks or staining.
Later finds, including a canine tooth in 1913, seemed to settle the debate.
A real ancestor dismissed.
The forgery did real damage.
In 1924 the Australian-born anatomist Raymond Dart, working in South Africa, identified a small fossil skull from a quarry at Taung.
In 1925 he argued in Nature that this ‘Taung Child’ belonged to an early human relative, which he named Australopithecus africanus.
It had the opposite combination to Piltdown: a small, apelike brain but humanlike teeth and signs of upright posture.
Many leading experts dismissed it, partly because it clashed with Piltdown's big-brain-first story.
It took more than two decades, and many further fossil discoveries in Africa, before Dart's view was widely accepted.
We now know that upright walking came long before large brains.
Exposed in 1953.
As genuine fossils emerged, Piltdown looked out of place.
In 1949 Kenneth Oakley applied a new fluorine test, which helps estimate how long bones have been buried.
The Piltdown bones contained surprisingly little fluorine, suggesting they were far younger than claimed.
In 1953 Oakley, with Joseph Weiner and Wilfrid Le Gros Clark, announced the truth.
The jaw came from an orangutan, its teeth filed down to look humanlike.
The skull belonged to a modern human who had lived only centuries earlier.
The bones had been stained to look ancient.
For decades people argued over who did it, with suspects including Woodward and even Arthur Conan Doyle.
A 2016 study using DNA analysis and CT scanning pointed to a single forger, and Dawson was by far the most likely.
Lessons from a forgery.
Piltdown wasn't exposed because science is infallible; it was exposed because science keeps testing.
Better methods and new evidence eventually revealed what expectation had hidden.
But the story offers lessons well beyond fossils.
Be extra careful with evidence that confirms exactly what you, your team or your country hoped to find.
Ask whether anyone has examined the original data, rather than a summary or a copy.
Notice when crucial pieces of evidence are conveniently missing.
And remember that the anomaly that doesn't fit, like the Taung Child, may turn out to be the real discovery.
When an idea seems to explain everything you expected, that's a moment to look harder, not to relax.
The key idea: In 1912 bones from a Sussex gravel pit were announced as a vital human ancestor.
Part two. Ern Malley: the poet who never lived.
In 1944 an Australian magazine hailed the discovery of a brilliant dead poet.
He had been invented in a single afternoon by two bored soldiers.
Modernism under attack.
In the early 1940s, Australian art and literature were split between traditionalists and a younger crowd excited by modernism, the experimental style of writers such as T.
S.
Eliot and painters like Picasso.
At the centre of the avant-garde was Angry Penguins, a magazine co-founded in Adelaide in 1940 by Max Harris, who was still a teenager.
Melbourne patrons John and Sunday Reed backed it, and their circle included the painters Sidney Nolan and Albert Tucker.
It published surrealist-influenced poetry and argued that Australia needed to break with old forms.
To its critics, much of this poetry looked like pretentious nonsense that anyone could produce.
Two of them decided to test that idea.
An afternoon's invention.
James McAuley and Harold Stewart were young poets who disliked modernism and preferred traditional craft.
In 1943 both were serving in the army in Melbourne.
By their own account, they wrote a whole body of work in a single afternoon.

They opened books at random, including a dictionary, a collected Shakespeare, a dictionary of quotations and an American report on draining swamps to control mosquitoes, and wove the phrases into sixteen poems.
They deliberately included nonsense, false allusions and clumsy lines.
Then they invented an author: Ern Malley, a mechanic and insurance salesman who had supposedly died young in 1943, leaving his poems unpublished.
They titled the collection The Darkening Ecliptic.
The bait is taken.
The poems reached Harris with a covering letter from Ethel Malley, Ern's supposedly grieving sister, who said she did not understand them but wondered if they were any good.
Harris was thrilled.
He believed he had found a major poet who had died unrecognised, and in 1944 he devoted a special issue of Angry Penguins to Ern Malley, with a cover painting by Sidney Nolan inspired by the poems.
Some readers suspected a joke from the start.
Within weeks, journalists began investigating who Ethel and Ern really were.
In June 1944 the press revealed the truth, and McAuley and Stewart explained their experiment, declaring that the poems were deliberately meaningless.
Ridicule and a courtroom.
The story was a sensation, and newspapers across the country mocked Harris and modernism together.
Worse followed.
South Australian police charged Harris with publishing indecent material, pointing to lines in the Ern Malley poems and other contributions to the magazine.
The trial in Adelaide in 1944 became famous for its absurdity.
A police detective was asked to explain why certain words and images were immoral, and admitted he did not know what some of them meant.
Harris was convicted and fined five pounds.
Angry Penguins survived only a few more years.
For a while the episode seemed to prove what the hoaxers intended: that modernist poetry could not tell genuine art from random words.
The poet who outlived them.
Then something unexpected happened.
Over the following decades, many critics and poets argued that the poems were striking, with vivid images and an odd emotional power, however they were made.
Sidney Nolan returned to Ern Malley in his art for years, and the American poet John Ashbery was among the admirers.
Some suggested the hoaxers had, despite themselves, poured real talent and feeling into the work.
The poems have stayed in print ever since, and the hoax inspired later writing, including Peter Carey's 2003 novel My Life as a Fake.
Does a poem's value depend on what its author intended?
Meaning kept appearing where the authors said there was none.
Some historians argue the hoax set Australian modernism back by years.
Max Harris went on to a long career as a bookseller, publisher and columnist, and never fully disowned Ern.
The key idea: In the 1940s Australian modernists around Angry Penguins argued for a break with old forms, and traditionalist critics thought the new poetry was nonsense.
Part three. Art forgery: the con artists who fooled the experts.
One forger sold a fake Vermeer to a Nazi leader.
Another was caught by a single tube of white paint.
The history of art forgery is full of daring tricks, and it raises a surprisingly hard question: why does a fake matter?
The forger who fooled Goring.
In May 1945 Dutch police arrested painter and dealer Han van Meegeren after a 'Vermeer' was traced from the collection of the senior Nazi Hermann Goring.
His defence was astonishing: it was not a national treasure, because he had painted it himself.
Disbelieving investigators had him paint a new 'Vermeer' under supervision.
In 1947 he was convicted of forgery and fraud, not collaboration, and sentenced to a year in prison, but died before serving it.
To some Dutch people he was a folk hero.
He invented religious scenes, as some experts thought Vermeer had an early religious phase.
He reused genuine seventeenth century canvases and mixed pigments with phenol-formaldehyde resin, the material of Bakelite, then baked the painting hard.
Rolling the canvas created cracks, and he rubbed ink into them.
In 1937 an expert hailed his Supper at Emmaus.
Inventing a collection.
German forger Wolfgang Beltracchi may have been even more ambitious.
Instead of copying known paintings, he created works that might plausibly have existed, often filling gaps where a real artist's painting was recorded in a catalogue but lost.
Just as important was the paperwork.
He and his wife invented a story that the pictures came from her grandfather's collection, and faked an old photograph of her posing as her own grandmother in front of several forgeries.
For years the works passed through auction houses and dealers, sometimes selling for millions.
His undoing was science.
One painting supposedly from 1914 contained titanium white, a pigment not yet available to artists then.
In 2011 he was sentenced to six years in prison.
Science and the trained eye.
Today suspicious paintings are examined like crime scenes.
Many pigments have known invention dates, so an impossible colour is a giveaway.
X-rays reveal hidden layers, infrared shows the underdrawing, and tree-ring dating estimates when panel wood was cut.
Nuclear tests in the 1950s and 1960s spiked carbon-14 in the atmosphere, so plants grown afterwards carry a modern signature that old materials do not.
Before laboratories, authenticity rested on connoisseurs, who knew an artist's hand like a friend's handwriting.
That still matters, but experts can be swayed by what they hope to find, and by a convincing provenance, the history of ownership.
A large scandal at New York's Knoedler gallery, which closed in 2011, showed that convincing paperwork and confident dealers could carry fakes into major collections.
Fakes closer to home.
Australia has not escaped.
A Brett Whiteley fraud case saw a conviction in 2016 overturned on appeal the following year, showing how hard forgery is to prove in court.
Aboriginal art faces its own problems.
Because it is popular with tourists and collectors, cheap imitations with no connection to the communities and cultures they copy have been widespread.
This harms artists and misrepresents their culture.
Many Aboriginal art centres now supply certificates and keep careful records of who made each work.
If you are buying, it helps to look for works sold through community art centres or reputable dealers.
The Indigenous Art Code is a voluntary industry code worth checking.
Why does a fake matter.
Here is the puzzle.
When experts believed Van Meegeren's Supper at Emmaus was a Vermeer, they found it profound.
Once exposed, the same canvas seemed clumsy to many viewers, and its value fell dramatically.
The paint did not change, so what did?
One answer is that we value art partly as an achievement: a genuine Vermeer is a particular person solving particular problems in seventeenth century Delft, and a forgery fakes that history.
Another is that an artwork carries a connection to its maker, like a letter in someone's own handwriting.
Fraud also causes real harm to buyers and to an artist's reputation, since fakes can distort what we think an artist was like.
Forgery makes us ask what we really value in art.
The key idea: Han van Meegeren invented new 'Vermeers' and used baked synthetic resin to fake the hardness of age.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What did Woodward's reconstruction of Piltdown Man show?
Answer. A humanlike braincase and an apelike jaw.
Question two. What did the hoaxers believe about modernist poetry?
Answer. That it was pretentious nonsense anyone could write.
Question three. Why did Van Meegeren mix his paint with synthetic resin and bake the painting?
Answer. To harden fresh paint so it seemed centuries old.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
